notes.b: Science is both a body of knowledge and a process for building it. It explains the natural world using evidence gathered by observation and experiment, and that evidence requirement is what separates scientific claims from opinions.
points: A scientific claim must be testable against evidence from the natural world. Questions of value or morals, such as “should we clone animals?”, can be informed by science but cannot be answered by it, because no experiment can measure what is right or wrong.

Scientific knowledge is evidence-based (empirical): ideas are accepted because they agree with observations and experimental results, not because of who proposed them. A famous name does not make an idea correct.

An observation is what is directly detected with the senses or instruments, such as “the broth went cloudy”. An inference is an explanation drawn from an observation, such as “microorganisms grew in the broth”. Scientists keep them separate, as an inference can be wrong when the observation is right.
notes.tip: If a question asks you to tell an observation from an inference, the observation is what was detected and the inference is the explanation for it.

notes.b: Scientific ideas are never declared final, yet the best of them last for generations. Two ideas explain why: ideas are open to revision, and they must be capable of being shown wrong.
points: Scientific knowledge is tentative but durable: any idea can be revised if new evidence contradicts it, yet well-tested ideas survive for a long time. The cell theory (the idea that all living things are made of cells) has survived more than 150 years of testing.
Tentative does not mean weak or a guess. It means the idea is held open to revision, while still being backed by a large amount of evidence.

An idea must be falsifiable: it must be possible, in principle, to imagine an observation that would show the idea is wrong. The philosopher Karl Popper made falsifiability his test of whether an idea is scientific.
Evidence can support an idea or refute it, but it can never prove an idea true for all time, because a later observation might contradict it. One reliable contrary result can disprove an idea.
notes.tip: Never write that a hypothesis or theory has been “proven”. Say the evidence supports it, or refutes it.

notes.h: The usual cycle of science: from observation to data
notes.b: Textbooks sometimes present “the scientific method” as a fixed recipe, but real science is messier. The first half of the usual cycle takes a scientist from noticing something to having data.
points: There is no single fixed scientific method. The process is often complex and iterative (it loops back on itself), following many different paths, but it usually involves the stages below.
1. Observation: the scientist notices something in the natural world.
2. Question: the scientist asks why or how it happens.
3. Hypothesis: a proposed, testable explanation is put forward.
4. Prediction: the scientist works out what should be found if the hypothesis is correct.
5. Experiment or further observation: the prediction is tested.
6. Collection and analysis of data: results are gathered and worked on to see what they show.
notes.tip: A past question asks for the stages that follow designing an experiment. Your answer should start with carrying out the experiment, collecting results and analysing them, which are steps 5 and 6 here, and then continue with the later stages: conclude, repeat, compare, publish, peer review and theory or law. The principles of a good experiment belong to Designing and conducting investigations.

notes.h: The usual cycle of science: from conclusion to theory
notes.b: Once the data is in, the work is not finished. The second half of the cycle checks the result and shares it, so that other scientists can judge it.
points: 7. Conclusion: the hypothesis is judged to be supported or rejected by the data.
8. Repetition and checking: the work is repeated, so that one odd result is not relied on.
9. Comparison with existing knowledge: the result is set against what is already known.
10. Publication in a scientific journal after peer review, which means other experts check the work before it is published.
11. Testing of the findings by other scientists, who try to confirm or challenge them.
12. Over time, well-supported findings are developed into a theory or law.
A rejected hypothesis leads to a new or modified hypothesis, so the cycle starts again. This is why the process is a loop and not a straight line.

Diagram: the cycle drawn as a loop with arrows. Labels: observation, question, hypothesis, prediction, experiment, data analysis, conclusion, repeat and check. Arrow from “hypothesis rejected” back to “new hypothesis”; “publish and peer review” leading out to “theory or law”.
notes.tip: You can be asked to outline the stages that follow designing an experiment. Give them in order: carry out, collect results, repeat, analyse, conclude, relate to existing knowledge, publish, peer review, then theory or law.

notes.h: Not all science is experimental, and science is creative
notes.b: The cycle suggests that every investigation is a laboratory experiment, but that is only one way of testing ideas. Science also needs imagination.
points: Not all science is experimental. Some fields test ideas by observation and comparison, for example fossil records and comparative anatomy as evidence for evolution, or field surveys of ecosystems.

Science is creative: imagining hypotheses and designing ways to test them takes imagination, and chance observations can start new lines of work, such as the discovery of penicillin, the standard example. There is more on this in Science, scientists and society.

notes.b: No scientist works alone for long. Science is a shared activity in which claims are expected to face challenge.
points: Scientists work in teams, build on others’ published work and expect their claims to be checked and challenged, because a claim that survives checking is more reliable.
Scepticism means doubting a claim until the evidence for it is good. It is a norm of science, not a personal attack on the scientist. There is more on this in Science as a global enterprise.

notes.b: Scientists are human, so the way science is done reflects the world they live in.
points: Science is influenced by the society, culture, funding and technology of its time, which affect what questions get investigated and what can be measured.
Individual scientists can be biased. There is more on the types of bias in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.

notes.b: The scientific method is powerful, but it has limits. Knowing them helps you judge how far a result can be trusted.
points: Limited by current knowledge and technology: some questions cannot yet be investigated. Cells could not be observed until microscopes were invented, and the internal structure of organelles could not be observed until electron microscopes were available.
The basis of the investigation may be wrong: if the theory or assumption a hypothesis rests on is false, the conclusions may be false too.
Human error and interpretation: data can be misread, and scientists can interpret the same results in different ways.
Experimental design: a poorly designed experiment can give results that seem to support a hypothesis when they do not. There is more on this in Designing and conducting investigations.

Applying results to nature: conditions in a laboratory are simpler and more controlled than in a living organism or an ecosystem, so results may not apply outside the laboratory. A drug that works on cells in a dish may not work in a person.
Science cannot answer questions of value, ethics or the supernatural, and it cannot prove a hypothesis absolutely, because evidence can only support or refute an idea.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to state a limitation. Pick one and give its reason, for example that a laboratory is simpler than a living organism, so results may not apply to nature.

notes.b: A hypothesis is the first step from an observation towards an explanation. It is the lowest-status kind of scientific idea, since it has yet to be tested.
points: A hypothesis is a proposed, testable explanation for an observation. It makes predictions that can be checked by experiment or observation.
A hypothesis may be supported or rejected; it is never proved.

Example: in the early 1980s Robin Warren and Barry Marshall proposed that stomach ulcers are caused by infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, not by stress and excess acid as was then believed. There is more on writing a testable hypothesis in Questioning and predicting.
notes.tip: To define a hypothesis, say it is a proposed (or possible) explanation for an observation that can be tested.

notes.h: Theories: the cell theory and other examples
notes.b: In everyday speech “theory” means a hunch. In science it means the opposite: the most thoroughly tested kind of explanation.
points: A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation of a wide range of observations, supported by many confirmed hypotheses and by evidence from many independent sources.
A theory explains why something happens and makes predictions. It is the highest status an explanation reaches in science.
A theory is not a guess, so the everyday phrase “just a theory” misuses the word.
The cell theory states that all living things are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life, and that all cells come from pre-existing cells.

Matthias Schleiden proposed in 1838 that plants are made of cells. Theodor Schwann extended this to animals in 1839. Rudolf Virchow added in 1855 that all cells arise from existing cells (“omnis cellula e cellula”).

Other biological theories include the theory of evolution by natural selection, proposed by Darwin and Wallace, and the germ theory of disease, which holds that many diseases are caused by microorganisms. There is more on the first in The theory of evolution by natural selection.
notes.tip: Don’t say a theory is a guess, and don’t say it is proven. A theory is a well-tested explanation that the evidence supports.

notes.b: A law is a different kind of knowledge from a theory. Where a theory explains, a law describes a pattern.
points: A law, or principle, is a statement, often mathematical, that describes a pattern that always occurs under stated conditions. It describes what happens but does not explain why.
Biology has few laws because living systems are variable, so patterns rarely hold without exception.

Mendel’s laws of segregation and independent assortment describe how alleles (versions of a gene) pass to offspring. They have known exceptions, for example linked genes. There is more on this in Mendel's Laws.
The laws of thermodynamics apply to living things. Energy is not created or destroyed, only converted, as when light energy is converted to chemical energy in photosynthesis.

notes.b: Examiners now ask you to tell these three apart. They differ in scope, purpose and the evidence behind them, and none is a stage on the way to another.
points: Scope: a hypothesis concerns one observation, a theory covers a wide range of observations, and a law covers one pattern.
Purpose: a hypothesis proposes an explanation, a theory gives a tested explanation, and a law describes a pattern.
Evidence: a hypothesis has little or none yet, a theory rests on a large body of evidence from many independent sources, and a law is repeated observation without exception under stated conditions.
All three can be revised or rejected if the evidence demands it.

A theory does not grow up into a law: they are different kinds of knowledge. A law describes a pattern and a theory explains it. A theory can explain a law; for example, Mendel’s laws are explained by the behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis.

A scientific fact is a repeatable observation, for example “DNA is found in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells”. A model is a simplified representation used to explain or predict. There is more on this in Models.
notes.tip: A common mistake is saying a theory becomes a law once it has enough evidence. Say instead that a law describes a pattern and a theory explains it.

notes.b: Because scientific knowledge is tentative, it changes over time. The cases that follow show this in action.
points: Ideas change because of new evidence that the old idea cannot explain, new technology that allows new observations (for example microscopes and DNA sequencing), reinterpretation of existing evidence, and replication (repeating of the work) by other scientists.
Change is usually gradual refinement. Occasionally a whole framework is replaced; the historian Thomas Kuhn called this a paradigm shift, in his book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe how a scientific idea has changed over time. For each case, give the old idea, the new evidence, the new idea and why it was accepted.

notes.h: Spontaneous generation gave way to biogenesis
notes.b: For a long time people believed that small creatures could appear from non-living matter. Two careful experiments, a couple of centuries apart, showed otherwise.
points: Old idea (spontaneous generation): living things such as maggots and microorganisms arise from non-living matter.
In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars that were open, sealed or covered with gauze. Maggots appeared only on the meat in the open jars, which flies could reach.
In the gauze-covered jars, flies laid their eggs on the gauze, not on the meat, so no maggots appeared.
In the early 1860s Louis Pasteur boiled broth in swan-neck flasks, which have an S-shaped neck. Air could enter, but dust and microorganisms were trapped in the bend, and the broth stayed clear.
When the neck was broken off, or the broth was tipped into the bend, microorganisms grew in it. This showed the microorganisms came from the dust and not from the broth itself.
New idea: living things come only from other living things (biogenesis), which supported the germ theory.

notes.h: The cell theory was built up over time
notes.b: The cell theory was not announced in one go. It grew as better microscopes let scientists observe more.
points: The cell theory (all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells) was built up by several scientists over decades as microscopes improved.
It is still being extended. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have been found to contain their own DNA.

notes.h: Stomach ulcers: a bacterium replaces stress as the cause
notes.b: This case shows how a well-established belief was overturned by a bacterium that doctors thought could not exist in the stomach.
points: Old idea: ulcers are caused by stress, spicy food and excess acid, and no bacterium could survive stomach acid.
Warren observed curved bacteria in biopsies (small samples of tissue) of inflamed stomach linings. Marshall and Warren cultured (grew in the laboratory) Helicobacter pylori in 1982.
In 1984 Marshall drank a culture of the bacteria, developed gastritis (an inflamed stomach lining) and treated it with antibiotics.
Other scientists repeated the findings, and trials showed that antibiotics cured most ulcers.
New idea: most stomach ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection and are treated with antibiotics.
Marshall and Warren received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005.
The case shows that a new idea is often resisted at first and is accepted when the evidence is reproduced.

notes.b: In this case the evidence was clear, yet the idea was ignored for years because nobody could say why it worked.
points: In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis, at Vienna General Hospital, noticed that far more mothers died of childbed (puerperal) fever on the ward run by doctors than on the ward run by midwives.
The doctors who ran that ward came from dissecting corpses, while the midwives did not.
He made staff wash their hands in chlorinated lime solution, and deaths fell sharply.
Many doctors rejected his idea because it lacked an explanation. It was accepted only after the germ theory of disease explained it.
The case shows that evidence without an explanatory theory can be ignored.

notes.h: Other ideas that changed in the same way
notes.b: The same pattern of old idea, new evidence and refined idea appears again in other topics in this course.
points: The five-kingdom system of classifying living things was replaced by three domains and six kingdoms.

The lock-and-key model of enzyme action was refined to the induced-fit model, and the membrane “sandwich” model was replaced by the fluid mosaic model. There is more on these in Domains of life, Classification and Models.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a hypothesis and a theory. Give a biological example of a theory.
questions.model: A hypothesis is a proposed, testable explanation for an observation. It makes predictions that can be checked by experiment or observation, and it may be supported or rejected but is never proved. A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation of a wide range of observations, supported by many confirmed hypotheses and by evidence from many independent sources. A theory explains why something happens and makes predictions, and it is not a guess. Example: the cell theory, which states that all living things are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life, and that all cells come from pre-existing cells.

questions.prompt: Using one named example, describe how a scientific idea in biology has been modified over time.
questions.model: Example: stomach ulcers. The old idea was that ulcers are caused by stress, spicy food and excess acid, and that no bacterium could survive stomach acid. Warren observed curved bacteria in biopsies of inflamed stomach linings, and Marshall and Warren cultured Helicobacter pylori in 1982. In 1984 Marshall drank a culture of the bacteria, developed gastritis and treated it with antibiotics. Other scientists repeated the findings, and trials showed that antibiotics cured most ulcers. The new idea is that most stomach ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection and are treated with antibiotics. The new idea was resisted at first and was accepted when the evidence was reproduced by others. It is supported by the evidence but, like every scientific idea, it remains open to revision if new evidence appears. Marshall and Warren received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005.

questions.prompt: State three limitations of the scientific method and explain each.
questions.model: First, the method is limited by current knowledge and technology: some questions cannot be investigated until new tools exist, e.g. cells could not be seen until microscopes were invented and the internal structure of organelles could not be seen until electron microscopes were available. Second, human error and interpretation: data can be misread, and scientists can interpret the same results in different ways. Third, applying results to nature: laboratory conditions are simpler and more controlled than in a living organism or ecosystem, so a result found in a laboratory may not apply outside it. For example, a drug that works on cells in a dish may not work in a person. Other limitations include the possibility that the basis of an investigation is wrong, poor experimental design, and the fact that science cannot answer questions of value, ethics or the supernatural.
